query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In near‐equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, small amounts of Al induce localized chemical ordering via atomic-size mismatch and electronic differences, which lowers the stacking fault energy locally and drives the formation of ordered L12 nanoprecipitates within a dominated FCC matrix. This dual-phase microstructure simultaneously enhances high-temperature strength (through precipitate and grain-boundary strengthening), provides effective sinks for radiation‐induced defects, and maintains cryogenic toughness via sustained FCC ductility and twinning.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, disordered FCC Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with near-equiatomic composition.
generation.intervention: Adjust the alloy’s Al content to a value near a critical threshold so that short-range chemical ordering is induced without triggering large-scale brittle intermetallics.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under high-temperature conditions (e.g., >500 °C) to assess strength retention, under radiation exposure to test defect absorption, and at cryogenic temperatures (≈77 K) to evaluate toughness and deformation mechanisms.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence and distribution of nanoscale ordered (L12-type) precipitates embedded in the overall FCC matrix, as mediated by Al-induced lattice distortions.
generation.mechanism: Al atoms, because of their size and electronic disparities relative to Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni, create localized regions of short-range order. This lowers the local stacking fault energy and promotes the nucleation of small ordered precipitates (e.g., L12 phase) within the FCC matrix. The precipitates enhance high-temperature strength (by impeding dislocation motion) and act as defect sinks to improve radiation tolerance, while the retained FCC matrix continues to favor ductile deformation (including twinning) at cryogenic temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: HEAs with Al content at or slightly above the threshold will develop a mixed microstructure with nanoscale ordered L12 precipitates in an FCC matrix. This structure will show superior high-temperature strength, environmental and radiation resistance, and improved cryogenic toughness compared to a lower-Al alloy that remains a fully disordered FCC phase.
generation.baseline: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA with lower Al content that remains as a single-phase disordered FCC structure, exhibiting lower high-temperature strength and reduced radiation tolerance and cryogenic ductility.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs within a limited Al content window; excessive Al may shift the balance toward undesirable brittle intermetallic phases, while too little Al will not produce the necessary local chemical ordering.
generation.uncertainty: The exact Al threshold for optimal short-range ordering and its quantitative impact on stacking fault energy, as well as the interplay with magnetic effects or other minor elements, remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs: one with Al content near the proposed ordering threshold and one with lower Al content (baseline). Subject both sets to identical thermal treatments, radiation exposures, and cryogenic mechanical testing, and use high-resolution microscopy (TEM and atom probe tomography) to characterize the presence of ordered L12 precipitates and measure stacking fault energy.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (TEM, atom probe tomography) to detect L12 ordering
High-temperature tensile or creep tests to assess strength retention
Radiation exposure tests followed by defect density measurement
Cryogenic fracture toughness and ductility tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-Al alloy does not develop discernible short-range ordered precipitates (or shows no significant difference in stacking fault energy) and fails to demonstrate improved high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, or cryogenic toughness relative to the low-Al baseline, then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic (fcc) structure to hexagonal-close-packing (hcp) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures.
